mcqs.question: A video-transcoding operation typically takes 5-15 minutes. Why is holding the HTTP connection open for the full duration a bad approach, even if timeouts are extended to allow it?
options: It isn't actually a bad approach — extending the timeout is a perfectly sufficient fix
HTTP technically forbids connections lasting longer than 60 seconds
It ties up a server worker for the entire duration and is fragile to any intermediate network failure, with no way for the client to resume afterward
The only issue is that it uses more bandwidth than a job/status pattern
mcqs.explanation: A long-held connection consumes server capacity for its whole duration (multiplying across concurrent requests) and is exposed to any load balancer, proxy, or network hiccup killing it mid-flight with no way to resume — the client would have to restart the whole operation. HTTP has no universal 60-second connection cap; the core problem is resource-holding and fragility, not primarily bandwidth.

mcqs.question: A mobile app has no public, reachable endpoint but keeps a foreground connection open while a user waits for a report to finish. Which completion-notification approach fits, per the compare slide?
options: A webhook on completion, since it's always the most efficient option
Polling only, since mobile apps can never use a stream-based approach
A status stream (or polling as a simpler fallback) — the app is a live, connected client without a reachable inbound endpoint
None of these — the operation must be made synchronous instead
mcqs.explanation: The compare slide is explicit that a webhook needs a reachable public endpoint the consumer can host, which a mobile app in this scenario doesn't have — a stream fits an already-connected live client well, with polling as the simpler fallback. Webhooks aren't 'always most efficient' when the receiving side can't host one, and making the operation synchronous is exactly the pattern this topic argues against for long operations.

mcqs.question: A job-status endpoint returns only {"failed": true} when a job fails, with no further detail. What's missing according to the status-resource design guidance?
options: Nothing — a boolean failed flag is sufficient information for any client
A structured error reason (machine-readable code plus human-readable message) so a client or support engineer can actually act on the failure
The response should instead retry the job automatically instead of reporting failure
The job's progress percentage is the only thing that should ever be included on failure
mcqs.explanation: A bare boolean tells a client something went wrong but gives no actionable information about what or why — the same structured-error thinking used for synchronous failures (a code plus a message) applies here too. Automatic retry is a separate design decision, not a substitute for reporting the failure reason, and progress alone doesn't explain why it failed.

mcqs.question: A team argues that setting a 10-minute HTTP timeout is 'simpler' than building a job/status endpoint pattern for a slow report-generation feature. What's the flaw in that reasoning?
options: There's no flaw — a longer timeout is strictly simpler and just as reliable
The flaw is only that 10 minutes is too short; a 30-minute timeout would fully resolve it

The long connection ties up server capacity the whole time and can't survive an intermediate network failure, leaving the client no way to resume — the job/status pattern trades a bit of API surface for real resilience
HTTP simply does not support timeouts longer than 60 seconds, making this approach technically impossible
mcqs.explanation: The 'simpler' long-timeout approach looks simpler only until something in the network path fails mid-request, at which point the client has no way to resume and must restart from scratch, and it ties up server workers the entire time regardless of failure. No specific timeout duration fixes the structural fragility, and HTTP itself doesn't cap connection duration at 60 seconds.
